State of Washington v. Ladson
facts: Police officers followed a car in which petitioner Edward Ladson was a passenger, recognizing the driver of the car as an individual suspected of involvement in gang activity. After stopping the car because its license tags were expired and subsequently arresting the driver for driving with a suspended license, a search of Ladson's person revealed illegal drugs and a stolen firearm. The Superior Court for Thurston County ordered the suppression of all evidence obtained from the search of Ladson, ruling that the search was unconstitutional as the traffic stop that had precipitated it was pretextual as the true reason the car had been stopped was not its expired license tags but rather to obtain evidence linking the driver to gang activity. The Washington Court of Appeals reversed the trial court's decision on the basis of the decision the United States Supreme Court had issued in the interim in Whren v. United States, which held that searches incident to pretextual traffic stops do not violate the United States Constitution. Ladson appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does the Washington State Constitution (Article I §7) provide broader protection against pretextual traffic stops than does the United States Constitution?
conclusions: Justice Sanders' opinion for the Court held that searches precipitated by pretextual traffic stops are unreasonable under the Washington State Constitution. The Court concluded that to rule otherwise would permit a triumph of form over substance that would create a substantial exception to the requirement that probable cause be established in order to conduct a search. Although the United States Supreme Court had decided that searches precipitated by pretextual stops are not inconsistent with the United States Constitution, the Court held that its own precedent had clearly established that the Washington State Constitution offers broader protection against searches and seizures that renders such searches unreasonable.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

State of Washington v. McCorkle
facts: Respondent Edward McCorkle was convicted of robbery in the Superior Court for Pierce County and sentenced to 171 months in prison on the basis of an offender score of 10 calculated by including 7 out of state convictions whose validity had been contested by McCorkle. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals concluded that although McCorkle had made only a general objection to the inclusion of the contested prior convictions, challenges to offender score calculations may be raised for the first time upon appeal. Upon turning to the merits of McCorkle's challenge, the Court of Appeals reversed the trial court's sentencing decision, holding that the contested out of state convictions were not comparable to Washington felonies and therefore not properly included. The state of Washington appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: May challenges to offender score calculations be raised for the first time upon appeal?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson's opinion for the Court held that McCorkle did not waive his right to contest the trial court's offender score calculation by raising only a general objection to the inclusion of his out of state convictions. The Court held that a clear burden of proof is placed upon the state to prove the existence and classification of prior convictions and objection is not required to hold the state to this standard.

State of Washington v. Aho
facts: Petitioner Fonua Aho was convicted of child molestation and rape in the Superior Court for King County. Aho subsequently appealed his conviction, asserting that convicting him for violating §9A.44.083 violated the prohibition against ex post facto laws in both the United States Constitution (Article 1 §10) and the Washington State Constitution (Article 1 §23) as he had been convicted on the basis of conduct spanning an eight-year period from 1987 through 1995 and §9A.44.083 had not taken effect until 1988. Thus, as the jury had not been asked to identify precisely when the acts giving rise to the conviction had occurred, Aho claimed that the possibility that he had been convicted for acts that preceded the effective date of the relevant statute violated his due process rights. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Aho's conviction, holding that §9A.44.083 merely recodified the prohibition against conduct already prohibited by its predecessor statute. Aho appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did Aho's conviction constitute an ex post facto application of the law?
conclusions: Justice Madsen's opinion for a unanimous Court reversed Aho's conviction, concluding that §9A.44.083 did not simply recodify the same offense already prohibited by the indecent liberties statute that preceded it as it had different age and age differential elements. Therefore, as §9A.44.083 represented a new statute rather than a recodification and could not be applied to conduct preceding its 1988 effective date, convicting Aho without requiring that the jury specify the date on which the acts giving rise to his conviction occurred violated Aho's right to due process.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

Enterprise Leasing, Inc. v. City of Tacoma
facts: Petitioner Enterprise Leasing filed suit in the Superior Court for Pierce County seeking a declaratory judgment that the city of Tacoma's attempt to assess its income at the higher local business and occupation tax rate applied to services rather than the local business and occupation tax rate applied to retail sales was invalid insofar as it was inconsistent with the definitions of retail sales and services established by state law. The Superior Court for Pierce County granted summary judgment to Enterprise Leasing and ordered the company's income to be assessed at the lower retail sales rate. On appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed the trial court's decision, holding that the city of Tacoma was not prohibited from defining retail sales differently than the state. Enterprise Leasing appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: May local governments define the term "retail sales" differently than the state for the purposes of assessing business and occupation taxes?
conclusions: Justice Smith's opinion for a unanimous Court ruled that local governments may generally define taxation categories as they see fit unless expressly constrained by a statute or constitutional provision. Thus, as Washington Revised Code §35.21.710, in defining "retail sales" for state purposes, did not expressly state that it was exclusive and superseded other definitions of "retail sales," the city of Tacoma was free to define the term in other ways.
